case_source: Against the judgment and decree dated 9-11-2006 passed by learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Brahmanbaria in Title Suit No. 26 of 2005.
full_judgment:
Md Emdadul Huq J : This first Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-11-2006 by which the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Brahmanbaria dismissed Title Suit No. 26 of 2005.

2. In that suit, the plaintiffs and two sets of defendants raised claim to the suit land as follows:

Plaintiff-appellants' case: The appellants, as plaintiffs, filed the above noted suit for declaration of their title to the suit land measuring a total of 1.79 acres comprising 35 decimals of the entire 1st suit plot being CS plot No. 338 and 1.44 acres of the 2nd suit plot being CS plot No. 340. The suit land has been fully described with further description in the schedule to the plaint.

3. Plaintiffs have stated that their grandmother's father Khorrom Hajee was the owner and CS recorded tenant of the suit land. The 1st suit Plot (CS 338) was solely owned and possessed by Khorrom Hajee. In the second suit plot (CS 340) Khorrom Hajee had eight annas share amounting to 1.255 acres. However, by virtue of an amicable partition, Khorrom Hajee used to possess a little larger part, namely 1.45 acres out of the 2nd suit plot.

4. Khorrom Hajee had no son and, on his death, his property including the suit land devolved upon his only brother Abdul Majid and 6 (six) daughters, Mohor Chan and 5 others. There was an amicable partition among the said heirs of Khorrorn Hajee, and his daughter Mohor Chan was allocated the suit land.

5. On the death of Mohor Chan, the suit land devolved upon her son Mohammad All (now deceased) and two other sons and one daughter, being proforma-defendant Nos. 29-31. However, there was an amicable partition among the said children of Mohor Chan and the suit land was allocated to her son Mohammad Ali.

6. On the death of Mohammad Ali, his three sons i.e. the present three plaintiffs and six daughters, being proforma-defendant Nos. 32-37, inherited the entire suit land. There was an amicable partition among the said children of Mohammad Ali and the three plaintiffs, as the Sons, got the suit land.

7. Proforma-defendant Nos. 22-28 are the heirs of Abdul Majid, brother of Khorrom Hajee. Proforma-defendant Nos. 38- 48 are the heirs of the 5 (five) other daughters of Khorrom Hajee i.e., the five sisters of Mohor Chan. These defendants have no claim over the suit land.

8. But the principal defendant Nos. 1- 21 have raised claims to the suit land as the successors-in-interest of some persons in whose names SA Khatian No. 51 has been wrongly prepared. Hence the suit.

Case of defendant No.13 (respondent):

9. He contends that the suit is not maintainable in its present form, that it is bad for defect of parties and also barred by limitation. He claims title to, and possession over, the entire 1st suit plot being CS Plot No. 33% measuring 35 decimals.

10. He admits that, the suit land originally belonged to CS recorded tenant Khorrom Hajee, who died leaving six daughters including Mohor Chan and brother Abdul Majid, as stated in the plaint.

11. He claims that Khorrom Hajee had another brother named Abdul Karim and that there was an amicable partition among the said heirs of Khorrom Hajee. In that amicable partition, the 1st suit plot (CS Plot No. 338) measuring 35 decimals was allocated to the said brother Abdul Karim and 1.44 acres of the 2nd suit plot (CS Plot No.340) was allocated to the said daughter Mohor Chan, the paternal grandmother of the plaintiffs. However Mohor Chan, during her life time, sold out her entire share of 1.44 acres to the predecessors of defendant Nos. 1-10.

12. He further claims that Abdul Karim, brother of Khorrom Hajee, died leaving two sons named Abdul Aziz, being the husband of Mohor Chan and paternal grandfather of the plaintiffs, and another son named Abdul Alim and one daughter named Multi Begum. By virtue of an amicable partition with the said brother and sister, Abdul Alim got the suit plot being CS plot No.338 measuring 35 decimals.

13. On the death of Abdul Alim, his 4 sons, being defendant Nos. 11-14, and another son Renu Bhuyian and two daughters inherited the 1st Suit plot. Upon amicable partition among the said heirs of Abdul Alim (son of Abdul Karim), defendant No. 13 got the entire 1st suit plot and he is in possession thereof. The latest BS Khatian No. 280 has been accordingly prepared in the name of defendant No. 13.

Case of defendant Nos. 1 and 4-7 and 10 (respondents):

14. They contend that the suit is not maintainable in its present form, that it is bad for defect of parties and also barred by limitation.

15. Like defendant No.I3, these defendants have stated the same genealogy of inheritance, namely that Khorrom Hajee, the original owner, died leaving the 6 (six) daughters including Mohor Chan and two brothers named Abdul Majid and Abdul Karim and that Mohor Chan acquired 1.44 acres of the 211 suit plot as a result of an amicable partition among the said heirs of Khorrom Hajee.

16. They claim title to and possession over the entire 2nd plot (CS plot No. 340) by virtue of a registered deed of permanent lease (ralcu:ir aqio) executed by Mohor Chan on 24-5-1957 and registered on 12-9-1957 in favour of Abdul Majid Molla, being the paternal grandfather of these defendants.

17. They claim that, before the said transfer document of 1957, their predecessor Idrish, Shahidul and Abdul Alim, being the three sons of Abdul Majid, (brother of Khorrom Hajee), had purchased 51.5 decimals out of the 2nd suit plot No. 340 from Mohammad Ali, the father of the plaintiffs. The said three sons of Abdul Majid was under an impression that Mohammad All had acquired the same by virtue of an oral gift from Khorrom Hajee. But, being suspicious of the oral gift, their father Abdul Majid obtained the transfer document of 1957 from Mohor Chan herself for the entire share of Mohor Chan amounting to 1.44 acres of the 2nd suit plot in favour of Abdul Majid and his three sons.

18. These defendants have further stated that their grandfather Abdul Majid, after acquiring the said 1.44 acres from Mohor Chan, equally distributed the same among his four sons, namely defendant No. 1 (Abdul Gafur), Idrish Mia (father of defendant Nos. 2 and 3) Shahidul Islam (father of defendant Nos. 4-7) and Abdul Alim (father of defendant No. 8-10).

19. Their grandfather Abdul Majid Molla died leaving the said four sons and one daughter Shah Chan. There was an amicable partition among the children of Abdul Majid Molla and the four sons were allocated equal shares in the 1.44 acres of the 2nd suit plot. The sister Shah Chan was given some land in a non-disputed plot.

20. The said equal shares of the four sons of Abdul Majid have been correctly recorded in the four separate BS Khatians being Nos. 98, 50, 270 and 42 in the names of the defendants and they are in possession thereof.

Proceeding and decision of trial court:

21. The trial court took up five issues for determination, namely (1) maintainability of the suit, (2) limitation, (3) defect of party, (4) the relief prayed Tor by the plaintiffs; and (5) any other relief.

22. At the trial, both sides adduced oral and documentary evidence. The trial Court, upon discussion of the evidence so adduced, decided that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their title and possession and dismissed the suit.

Deliberation in Appeal:

23. Mr Tabarak Hossain, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellants, submits that the plaintiffs are the grandsons of the admitted owner of the suit land i.e., Mohor Chan being one of the six daughters of the admitted original owner Khorrom Hajee.

24. Mr Hossain next submits that since the defendants claim that Mohor Chan had exhausted her interest in the suit land, particularly in the 2nd suit plot, by virtue of a transfer document registered in 1957, the burden of proof of that claim is on the defendants.

25. Mr Hossain next draws our attention to the said transfer document of 1957 (Exhibit-3) and refers to the various writings contained on the reverse of the 2nd and 3rd pages in the form of the report of the sub-Registrar, Brahmanbaria and the decision of the District Registrar, Dacca as recorded in 1957.

26. Mr Hossain next submits that these writings clearly show that, under direction of the then District Registrar, Dacca, the Sub-Registrar of Brahmanbaria conducted an inquiry on two occasions and reported that the executants of the deed Mohor Chan did not appear to admit the alleged execution of the deed by her and then the District Registrar recorded his decision under section 75 of the Registration Act, 1908 to the effect that the document had been duly executed and accordingly registered the same.

27. Mr Hossain next submits that since the admitted owner Mohor Chan never presented herself before the registering authority and thus denied the execution of that deed, no title passed to Abdul Majid, the transferee of that deed, being the predecessors of the defendant Nos. 1 and 4- 7 and 10.

28. Mr Hossain lastly submits that the oral evidence also support plaintiffs' possession over the suit land and therefore the Appeal should be allowed and the suit should be decreed.

29. In reply Mr Khair Ezaz Masud, the learned Advocate for the respondent-defendant Nos. 1 and 4-7 and 10, submits that the 1st set of contesting defendants, namely defendant No. 13, claims the 1st suit plot CS plot No. 338 measuring 35 decimals as the heirs of Abdul Karim, being one of the two surviving brothers of the admitted original owner Khorrom Hajee.

30. Mr Masud next submits that the plaintiffs, in their plaint are silent about the existence of Abdul Karim, but plaintiff No. 3, deposing as PW I, admitted such existence and further admitted that defendant No. 13 is one of the grandsons of the said Abdul Karim.

31. Mr Masud next submits that this very admission of PW 1 shows that the plaintiffs are not entitled to the entire suit land and that they would be entitled to a lesser quantum of share, because on the death of Khorrom Hajee his 6 (six) daughters including plaintiffs predecessor Mohor Chan were entitled to 2/3 share as Koranic heirs and the two brothers of Khorrom Hajee were entitled to the remaining 1/3 share as residuary and therefore the instant suit for simple declaration of title to the entire suit land is not maintainable.

32. Mr Masud next submits that the trial Court correctly and lawfully held that plaintiffs', predecessor Mohor Chan had exhausted her entire interest by virtue of the transfer deed (Exhibit-Kha) executed by Mohor Chan on 24-5-1957 and registered under order of the District Registrar on 12-9-1957.

33. Mr Masud next submits that, according to section 75 of the Registration Act, 1908 a District Registrar has the lawful authority to cause an inquiry in case of refusal by the executant of a deed to present the deed for registration.

34. Mr Masud next submits that, in the instant case, the District Registrar, Dacca had jurisdiction to cause the inquiry over the genuineness of the execution of the deed and he recorded his decision to register the said transfer document, because he was satisfied about the fact that the Mohor Chan, the executant, was found to be avoiding the presentation of the deed.

35. Mr Masud next submits that the other documents namely the RS Katian and the latest BS Khatians show that the predecessor of the contesting defendants, after acquisition of the suit land by virtue of the said transfer deed, were in possession and accordingly these records of right were prepared in their names and they have been paying rent.

36. Mr Masud lastly submits that the trial Court lawfully and correctly dismissed the suit and this appeal is liable to be dismissed. Discussion, findings and decision in Appeal:

37. The trial court framed five issues and discussed the merit of the claim of the parties and generally recorded its decision on all the issues together against the plaintiffs. This manner of recording general decision on the issues is not proper. So, in this judgment, we have recorded our decision on the individual issues as mandated by law.

38. With regard to the issue No. 2 on defect of party, the defendants have neither stated in their writer statement nor have they adduced any evidence in support of their claim. The materials on record do not show any defect of party. Moreover, this issue was not agitated at the hearing of this Appeal. So this issue is decided in favour of the plaintiffs.

39. The other issues being Nos.1 and 3, 4 and 5 on maintainability of the suit, limitation, plaintiffs' title and possession and the relief prayed for interlinked. So, these are taken up together and discussed in the following part of this judgment.

40. The pleadings of the parties show that the contesting defendants admit that the suit land originally belonged to Khorrom Hajee. This is further proved by the two CS Khatians, Exhibit-1 and Exhibit-1 (ka). The CS khatians show that the entire 1st suit plot and the eight anas of share in the suit holding including 2nd suit plot (340) were recorded in the name of Khorrom Hajee. Exhibit-1 (ka) further shows that the entire 2nd suit plot measuring 1.44 acres was possessed by Khorrom Hajee.

41. Plaintiffs have, in their plaint, stated that Kharrom Hajee left only one brother named Abdul Majid. But the defendants claim that Khorrom Hajee had, apart from Abdul Majid, another brother named Abdul Karim. In this respect plaintiff No.3, deposing as PW I on behalf of all the plaintiffs, in cross-examination, stated that

“খোররম আলী ভূঁইয়ার এক ভাইয়ের নাম আব্দুল মজিদ ভূঁইয়া; অপর ভাইয়ের লাম আব্দুল করিম ভূঁইয়া। আব্দুল আজীজ ভূঁইয়ার আরেক ভাই ছিলেন তাহার মাম ছিল আব্দুল আলীম ভূঁইয়া । আব্দুল আলীম ভূঁইয়ার পুক্রগণ হইতেছে ১১.১৪ নং বিবাদী ।.........আমার দাদী মোহর চানকে বিবাহ দেওয়া হয় আব্দুল করিম ভূঁইয়ার পুত্র আবদুল আজিজ ভূঁইয়ার নিকট”

42. The above statement of PW 1 clearly prove the existence of Abdul Karim as one of two surviving brothers of Khorrom Hajee. It follows that the six daughters of Khorrom Hajee, as Koranic heirs, inherited 2/3 (two-thirds) share, and the two brothers, as residuary heirs, inherited 1/3 (one third) share of the property left by Khorrom Hajee.

43. With regard to the time of death of Khorrorn Hajee and the events thereafter, not much evidence is available on record. However, SA Khatian No. 51, Exhibit- 2(kha), shows that the various plots of the earlier CS Khatian No.46, including the 2nd suit plot (CS 340) measuring 1.44 acres were recorded in the names of a number of persons. The name of Khorrom Hajee is not there in the said SA Khatian. Four of those SA recorded tenants are Mohor Chan, daughter of Khorrom Hajee and Abdul Alim, Sahidul Islam, and Idrish Ali, being the three sons of Abdul Majid i.e. the brother of Khorrom Hajee. So the SA Khatian indicates that CS tenant Khorrom died before preparation of the SA Khatian and that there was an amicable partition among the heirs of Khorrom Hajee and the 2nd suit plot, which was in possession of Khorrom Hajee as per CS record, fell in the share of the Mohor Chan.

44. The said SA Khatian further proves the truth of the purchase and possession of some land by the three sons of Abdul Majid. It is noted that the 2nd set of defendants claim that the said three sons of Abdul Majid were misled to purchase 51.5 decimals by kabala dated 9-4-1956 (Exhibit-ka) executed by the self declared owner Mohammad Ali, the son of Mohor Chan and father of the plaintiffs.

45. The defendants further claim that Abdul Majid, the father of the said three purchasers and the predecessor of the 2nd set of defendants, did not rely on that kabala and got a subsequent transfer deed of 1957 (Exhibit-Kha) executed by the Mohor Chan herself.

46. This subsequent transfer document (Exhibit-Kha) shows that it was executed by Mohor Chan by putting thumb impression and that the transfer has been described as চিরস্থায়ী রায়তী পত্তন in respect of the entire 2nd suit plot No. 340 in favour of Abdul Majid Mollah, the predecessor of the 2nd set of defendants.

47. However, on the reverse of the 2nd page of that document (Exhibit-Kha), the District Registrar, Dacca recorded his decision on 12-9-1957 and thereby appointed the Sub-Registrar, Brahmanbaria as the Commissioner under section 38 of the Registration Act, 1908 to ascertain as to whether the deed was executed by Mohor Chan. Accordingly, the Sub-Registrar, Brahmanbaria recorded the report as follows:

"Having visited the residence of one "Abdul Aziz Bhuiyan Shahib" of Suhilpur, Thana Brahmanbaria, District-Tripura, I have this day could not examine the said Mohar Chan Bibi W/O of Abdul Aziz Bhuiyan, as no such executant named as Mohar Chan Bibi was found at the residence as mentioned with petition."

48. After the said report, the District Registrar again directed the Sub-Registrar, Brahmanbaria to report on the matter. This time the Sub-Registrar reported as follows:

"Having visited the residence of Mohor Chan Bibi wife of Abdul Aziz Bhuiyan of Suhilpur, Thana Brahmanbaria, District-Tripura, religion Muslim, by profession-House wife, I have this day could not examine the said Mohor Chan Bibi, as she was found unwilling keeping out of the way in spite of due intimation which was proved to my satisfaction."

49. After the second report, as quoted above, the District Registrar, Dacca recorded his decision on the reverse of the 3rd page as quoted below:

"Admitted to registration u/s 75 of Act XVI of 1908 by order of the District-Registrar Dacca on 16-6-1958 in case No. 3, u/s 74 of 1908."

50. For considering the legality of the above decision of District Registrar, Dacca, section 38 of the Registration Act, 1908 is quoted below

"38. Persons exempt from appearance at registration office:

(1)(a) A person who by reason of bodily infirmity is unable without risk or serious inconvenience to appear at the registration-office, or

(b) a person in jail under civil or criminal process, or

(c) persons exempt by law from personal appearance in Court and who would but for the provision next hereinafter contained be required to appear in person at the registration-office.

shall not be required so to appear.

(2) In the case of every such person the registering officer shall either himself go to the house of such person, or to the jail in which he is confined, and examine him or issue a commission for his examination"

51. It is evident that section 38 empowers a Sub-Registrar to go to the residence of certain type of executants or to a convenient place for examining such executant.

<u>52. Sections 73 to 75 of the Registration Act, 1908 provide for a situation where an executant denies the execution or refuses to an executed deed for registration. Section 73 requires that, in such case, an application is to be filed to the Registrar, superior in rank and then the Registrar shall follow the procedure as laid down in sections 74 and 75, which are quoted below:</u>

<u>"74. Procedure of Registrar on such application.— In such case, and also where such denial as aforesaid is made before a Registrar in respect of a document presented for registration to him, the Registrar shall, as soon as conveniently may be, enquire."</u>

<u>(a) whether the document has been  executed:,</u>

<u>(b) whether the requirement of the law for the time being in force have been complied with on the part of the applicant or person presenting the document for registration, as the case may be, so as to entitle the document to registration."</u>

<u>75. Order by Registrar to register and procedure thereon:</u>

<u>(1) If the Registrar finds that the document bad been executed and that the said requirements have been complied with he shall order the document to be registered.</u>

<u>(2) If the document is duly presented for registration within thirty days after the making of such order, the registering officer shall obey the same and thereupon shall, so far as may be, practicable, follow the procedure prescribed in sections 58, 59 and 60.</u>

<u>(3) Such registration shall take effect as of the document had been registered when it was first duly presented for registration."</u>

<u>53. It is evident that section 75 empowers a Registrar (superior in rank) to cause an inquiry in a case where the executant denies the execution of a deed and refuses to present himself or herself before the registering authority (Sub-Registrar).</u>

54. In the instant case, the District Registrar, Dacca after causing an inquiry recorded his decision in favour of the transferee and the deed was accordingly registered. Section 75(3) provides that the deed so registered has all the legal effect of a regular deed, as if presented for registration.

55. In consideration of the 2nd inquiry report under section 38 as quoted earlier and the provisions of 73-75 of the Registration Act, 1908, we find no illegality or infirmity in the decision recorded by the District Registrar, Dacca. Accordingly we hold that the District Registrar lawfully exercised his authority in registering the deed in 1957 in the ordinary course of his official job. His action and decision were legal.

56. We further hold that the result of registration of the deed executed by Mohor Chan (Exhibit-Kha) is that her title to 1.44 acres of the 2nd suit plot CS 340 passed on to the transferee Abdul Majid, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1 and 4-7 and 10.

57. In the body of this transfer document the nature thereof is stated as "চিরস্থায়ী বন্দোবস্ত/পাট্টা দলিল” along with a statement about receipt of consideration and delivery of possession. So, it is essentially a sale deed and the said bangla expression indicating settlement বন্দোবস্ত/পাট্টা does not affect the passing of title.

58. The fact of passing of the title to Abdul Majid by virtue of the transfer document of 1957 is further evidenced by the collateral documents, namely the 4 (four) (Halkhatian) (Exhibit-Ga series) prepared in the names of the defendants and also by the rent receipts (Exhibit-Gha series) showing payment of rent by them for the years 1392 to 1412 BS.

59. On the possession aspect, the oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs and the 2nd set of contesting defendants through PWs 1-3 and DWs 1-4 respectively appear to be evenly balanced. But considered with the title documents, Exhibit-Ka and Kha, read with the SA khatian (Exhibit-2), the BS khatians Exhibit- (Ga-series) and the rent receipts, (Exhibits Gha-series), we hold that the testimony of the DWs are credible and that the said defendants are in possession of the 2nd suit plot.

60. The trial court's decision on disbelieving the title and possession of the plaintiffs is correct and lawful. We agree with that decision.

61. It is noted that the trial Court recorded a finding that the 1st suit plot being CS plot No. 338 has been recorded in the names of the defendant Nos. 11-14.

62. In respect of the said 1st suit plot, defendant No. 13 or the plaintiffs did not produce the SA Khatian or the certified copy of the BS Khatian or any rent receipt.

63. However, defendant No. 13 himself deposed as DW 2 and supported his claim. He also produced a copy of BS Khatian No.280 (Exhibit-A) comprising the single BS plot No. 569 measuring 35 decimals. This document contains the remark of the Union Revenue Assistant “রাজস্ব আদায়ের স্বার্থে বি এস খতিয়ানের অবিকল নকল কপি দেওয়া গেল।” This document is not the certified copy. But it contains the names of defendant No. 13 and his three brothers.

64. This document (Exhibit-A) read with our findings on the fact of inheritance of 1/3 share from Khorrom Hajee by his two brothers named Abdul Majid, the predecessor of 2nd set of defendants, Abdul Karim, grandfather of defendant Nos. 11-14, and the fact of inheritance of 2/3 share by the six daughters of Khorrom Hajee, and the admitted amicable partition among those heirs, and the corroborating fact of inclusion of the name of only Mohor Chan as the SA recorded tenant for the only 2nd suit plot and the failure of the plaintiffs to produce any SA Khatian in respect of the 1st suit plot and failure of the plaintiff to prove their possession over the 2nd suit plot, we hold that plaintiffs have failed to prove their exclusive title to, and possession over the 1st suit plot.

65. Accordingly we hold that the present suit for simple declaration of title is not maintainable. We further hold that since defendant Nos. 1 and 4-7 and 10 have been in possession of the 2nd suit plot since 1957, that is, since a time when plaintiffs predecessor Mohor Chan and her son Mohammad Ali were alive and were aware of the possession of the said defendants, the cause of action, if any, arose in 1957, when the defendants got into possession not as cosharers by inheritance from Khorrom Hajee but as the purchasers from the said Mohor Chan. The instant suit having been filed in 2006 is barred by limitation.

66. In view of the above findings, issue Nos. 1 3, 4 and 5 are decided against the plaintiffs.

67. We conclude that the trial court lawfully and correctly dismissed the suit. This appeal has no merit and hence liable to be dismissed.

68. Court fee paid is correct.

69. The appeal is dismissed on contest.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.
